short: The hound guarding the Greek underworld.
note: The monstrous dog guarding the entrance to Hades, commonly depicted with three heads. Bringing Cerberus to the upper world was the last of Heracles’ twelve labors.

short: Possibly Spenser’s alluring boatwoman in The Faerie Queene.
note: Possibly Phaedria, the pleasure-loving woman who ferries travelers across the Idle Lake in Book II of Edmund Spenser’s The Faerie Queene. The name is associated with Greek phaidros, “bright” or “cheerful.”

sources.label: Washington University: Spenser Archive, Book II, Canto VI

short: Possibly Portia’s attendant in The Merchant of Venice.
note: Possibly Nerissa, Portia’s attendant and confidante in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice. She accompanies Portia to Venice in disguise and marries Gratiano.

sources.label: Folger Shakespeare Library: The Merchant of Venice

short: Virginia Woolf’s 1921 collection of experimental short fiction.
note: A collection of eight short stories by Virginia Woolf, published by the Hogarth Press in 1921 with woodcuts by Vanessa Bell. It includes “Kew Gardens,” “A Haunted House,” and “A Society.”

sources.label: Smith College Libraries: Monday or Tuesday

short: James Branch Cabell’s imaginary medieval French province.
note: The setting of James Branch Cabell’s interconnected fantasies, collectively called the Biography of the Life of Manuel. Its name combines suggestions of Poitiers and Angoulême.

sources.label: Virginia Commonwealth University Libraries: Maps of Poictesme

short: The invented noble title in Puss in Boots.
note: In Charles Perrault’s Puss in Boots, a resourceful cat presents his poor master as the wealthy Marquis of Carabas and contrives to obtain a castle and royal marriage for him.

sources.label: Charles Perrault: Tales of Passed Time

short: The ancient southern supercontinent, also called Gondwana.
note: A former supercontinent that joined the landmasses now represented by South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India, and neighboring regions. Its breakup helped produce the modern arrangement of continents.

short: Possibly Roncesvalles, the Pyrenean pass associated with Roland.
note: Possibly the French name of Roncesvalles in the Pyrenees, associated with the defeat of Charlemagne’s rearguard in 778 and the medieval Song of Roland.

aliases: Law of the Irreversibility of Evolution
short: A historical principle of evolutionary irreversibility.
note: Louis Dollo’s principle that evolution does not exactly retrace its earlier course, often expressed as the improbability of regaining a lost complex feature. Modern research identifies exceptions to a strict ban on reacquisition.

sources.label: Elmer and Clobert: Dollo’s law in the post-genomic age

short: French: a street entertainer or acrobat.
note: A French word for an itinerant performer, acrobat, or fairground entertainer; also used figuratively for a buffoon or charlatan.

short: French: a maggot or small worm used as fishing bait.
note: A French word for a fly larva or maggot, particularly one used as fishing bait. Its ultimate origin is uncertain.

short: A Christian devotion recalling the Annunciation.
note: A Christian devotion recalling the Annunciation, traditionally recited morning, noon, and evening.

short: A small desert fox with very large ears.
note: A small desert fox distinguished by very large ears.

short: A low couch or cushioned seat.
note: A long, low couch, often without a back or arms.

short: A hard protective shell.
note: The hard protective covering over an animal’s back, especially the upper shell of a turtle.

short: In a quiet or lowered voice.
note: In a low, quiet voice.

short: Closely packed in rows.
note: Packed closely together in rows or ranks.

short: A small writing desk.
note: A small writing desk with drawers or compartments for papers.

short: A paid position requiring little work.
note: A paid position requiring little or no work.

short: A low barrier controlling water or fish.
note: A low dam or barrier across flowing water, used to divert or regulate it. A weir can also be a fence-like structure arranged to trap fish.

short: An ornamental arrangement of garden beds.
note: A formal arrangement of garden beds, often divided by paths and laid out in decorative patterns.

short: A water buffalo.
note: A carabao is a water buffalo. The name entered English through Philippine Spanish from a Visayan word, karabáw.

short: American science-fiction author and mathematician (1944–2024).
note: A science-fiction writer and mathematics professor whose work explored artificial intelligence, virtual worlds, and technological transformation. His books won multiple Hugo Awards.

sources.label: Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers Association: Vernor Vinge

short: Leon Trotsky, Russian revolutionary assassinated in exile in 1940.
note: A leading Bolshevik and organizer of the Red Army, later expelled from the Soviet Union after his struggle with Stalin. He was assassinated in Mexico in 1940 by a Soviet agent.

term: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
short: Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s poem about a seafarer’s transgression and ordeal.
note: Coleridge’s long supernatural poem follows a mariner who kills an albatross and survives a terrible voyage. The hermit and the ivy-covered cushion belong to its final section.

sources.label: Poetry Foundation: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

short: A bush or thick clump of ivy.
note: An old word for an ivy bush or dense growth of ivy; tod is a bush, tuft, or tangled mass of vegetation.

short: Spanish Carmelite mystic and poet (1542–1591).
note: A Carmelite reformer and religious poet whose writings describe spiritual purification, detachment, and union with God. His major works include The Ascent of Mount Carmel and The Dark Night.

sources.label: Vatican: Saint John of the Cross

short: Czech writer; the quotation comes from his account of a cat’s viewpoint.
note: The Czech writer Karel Čapek wrote the humorous essay From the Point of View of a Cat. Its feline narrator treats a human housemate as a source of warmth before returning to the voices outside.

sources.label: Karel Čapek: From the Point of View of a Cat (reprint)

term: Arms and the man I sing
short: The opening of Virgil’s Aeneid in John Dryden’s translation.
note: John Dryden’s rendering of Arma virumque cano, the opening of Virgil’s Aeneid. The epic follows Aeneas from fallen Troy to Italy, where his descendants are destined to found Rome.

sources.label: John Dryden: translation of Virgil’s Aeneid

short: The Cyclops blinded by Odysseus in the Odyssey.
note: A one-eyed giant, son of Poseidon, who traps Odysseus and his companions in a cave. Odysseus escapes by intoxicating and blinding him, then hiding his men beneath the giant’s sheep.

short: A one-eyed giant in Greek mythology.
note: Greek mythology includes several groups of Cyclopes: divine craftsmen associated with Zeus’s thunderbolts, and the pastoral giants encountered by Odysseus. Polyphemus belongs to the latter group.

sources.label: Theoi: classical sources on the Cyclopes

short: David Copperfield’s formidable but generous great-aunt.
note: A character in Charles Dickens’s David Copperfield. Though brusque and eccentric, she takes in the young David and becomes his protector and benefactor.

short: Charles Dickens’s novel of a boy’s growth into a writer.
note: Published in 1849–1850, Dickens’s first-person novel follows David’s childhood, education, friendships, work, and marriages. Its characters include Betsey Trotwood, Mr. Micawber, and Uriah Heep.

short: An ancient people of central Italy, influential on early Rome.
note: The people of Etruria, chiefly in present-day Tuscany and neighboring regions. Their cities, tombs, art, and inscriptions preserve evidence of a distinctive civilization gradually absorbed into Roman power.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Etruscan Art

short: The island civilization described by Plato as lost beneath the sea.
note: A powerful island state in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias. His account places it beyond the Pillars of Heracles and describes its destruction by earthquakes and flooding.

sources.label: Plato: Timaeus, MIT Internet Classics Archive

short: A legendary lost continent imagined in the Pacific.
note: A supposed sunken Pacific continent used in speculative explanations of ancient civilizations. It belongs to lost-continent speculation, rather than established geological history.

sources.label: Kenneth Macgowan: Early Man in the New World

short: Possibly Urania, the Greek Muse of astronomy.
note: Possibly the French form of Urania, the Muse associated with astronomy and the heavens. She is commonly represented with a celestial globe and a pointing rod.

short: Relating to Gregor Mendel’s principles of inheritance.
note: Named for Gregor Mendel, whose pea experiments established basic patterns of inheritance. Mendelian inheritance concerns traits transmitted according to such patterns, including dominant and recessive forms.

sources.label: National Human Genome Research Institute: Mendelian Inheritance

short: Women maintained by wealthy lovers; courtesans.
note: A historical French-derived term for courtesans or women supported by wealthy lovers. It comes from demi-monde, literally “half-world,” a socially disreputable circle bordering fashionable society.

short: French light infantry or cavalry; literally “hunters.”
note: Soldiers of French light infantry or light cavalry units, traditionally valued for speed and maneuverability. The word is the plural of chasseur, “hunter.”

short: French: master, teacher, or a professional title of respect.
note: A French word meaning master or teacher. It also serves as a title of address for certain professionals, especially lawyers.

short: French: “the mire” or “the mud.”
note: Fange is a literary French word for mire or mud, also used figuratively for degradation or moral filth. La is the feminine definite article, “the.”

short: Latin: time.
note: The Latin noun tempus means time, a period or occasion, and sometimes an appropriate moment or season.

short: A cave complex in southwestern France renowned for Paleolithic paintings.
note: A decorated cave in the Vézère Valley, discovered in 1940, whose walls preserve striking prehistoric images of animals. It forms part of a UNESCO World Heritage group of prehistoric sites.

sources.label: UNESCO: Prehistoric Sites and Decorated Caves of the Vézère Valley

short: A French village and district central to the study of prehistory.
note: Les Eyzies lies in the Vézère Valley of southwestern France, amid Paleolithic shelters, archaeological deposits, and decorated caves. Nearby sites form part of the valley’s World Heritage designation.

sources.label: UNESCO: Vézère Valley World Heritage documentation

short: French égouts: sewers or drains.
note: The French plural of égout, an underground sewer or drainage channel.

short: A Spanish cave famous for Paleolithic art.
note: The cave of Altamira in northern Spain preserves outstanding prehistoric paintings and engravings. It is a major example of Paleolithic cave art and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

sources.label: Spanish Ministry of Culture: Altamira World Heritage

short: A tough, fibrous variety of jade.
note: One of the two principal materials called jade, the other being jadeite. Nephrite consists of tightly intergrown amphibole fibers and occurs in colors including white and several shades of green.

sources.label: Office québécois de la langue française: nephrite

short: A recessed boundary wall that leaves a landscape view unobstructed.
note: A ditch containing a wall or fence below the normal ground level, creating a barrier without an ordinary above-ground fence breaking the view.

sources.label: Collins English Dictionary via Dictionary.com: ha-ha

short: Development from an unfertilized egg.
note: A form of reproduction in which an embryo develops from an egg without fertilization by a male reproductive cell.

short: Latin: “beware of the dog.”
note: A Latin warning meaning “beware of the dog.” A famous example accompanies the dog mosaic at the entrance to the House of the Tragic Poet in Pompeii.

short: Possibly Saint Anne, traditionally the mother of Mary.
note: Possibly Saint Anne, the traditional mother of the Virgin Mary and grandmother of Jesus. Her name and life come from early Christian apocryphal writings. Sainte Anne is the French form.

short: French: “Holy Cross.”
note: French for “Holy Cross”: sainte means holy or sacred, and croix means cross. The phrase commonly designates the cross of Christ in Christian place names and dedications.

short: Possibly Mimizan, a town on France’s Atlantic coast.
note: Possibly Mimizan, a coastal town in the Landes region of southwestern France. Its name closely resembles Mimizon; port is the French word for a harbor.

short: French: “House of the Dog.”
note: French for “House of the Dog”: maison means house, du means “of the,” and chien means dog.

short: Kate Wilhelm’s first science-fiction collection, published in 1963.
note: A collection of science-fiction stories by Kate Wilhelm, published in 1963. Its title tale first appeared in Astounding in April 1957.

short: Possibly the number of the beast in Revelation 13:18.
note: Possibly the number assigned to the beast in Revelation 13:18. The passage invites the reader to calculate a human name through its numerical value.

short: Possibly French culot: impudence or audacity.
note: Possibly the French noun culot, meaning impudence, cheek, or audacity. The same word can also mean the base or bottom of an object.

short: Egrets; the French name for these plume-bearing herons.
note: French aigrette names an egret, a long-legged heron noted for its fine plumes. The word also names a tuft of feathers or an ornament made from them.

short: A protective wrapping for the lower leg.
note: A strip of cloth wound around the leg between ankle and knee, formerly common in military dress; the word can also denote a gaiter. It comes from Hindi paṭṭī, “bandage.”

short: Payment for services or work.
note: A formal term for money received in return for work: a fee, salary, or other remuneration.

short: A small wreath worn as a crown.
note: A garland for the head, often made from flowers or leaves.

short: A low female vocal register.
note: The lowest conventional female singing voice, below mezzo-soprano; also a singer or musical part in that range.

short: Combing fibers before they are spun.
note: Cleaning and disentangling loose fibers with toothed implements or machines, gathering them together in preparation for spinning yarn.

short: A lump or small piece, especially of meat.
note: A chunk or portion of flesh or other material; by extension, a small fragment or extract.

short: Relating to tears or tear-producing glands.
note: Also spelled lacrimal: concerning tears and the glands that secrete them. Lachrymal fluid is tear fluid.

short: A formal pledge to fulfill an obligation.
note: A legally recorded undertaking, commonly a promise to appear before a court.

short: The military morning wake-up signal.
note: A call, commonly sounded on a bugle near sunrise, telling soldiers to rise or assemble for the day’s first formation.

short: A servant or attendant.
note: An older word for a servant, historically especially a male servant. It derives from Latin servire, “to serve.”

short: An open passage between buildings or their wings.
note: A passage beside or between parts of buildings. The word can also describe a sunken open space that gives a basement light, air, or an entrance.

short: Personal property rather than land or buildings.
note: Goods or possessions treated as personal property, distinguished from real estate. Historically, the word was also applied to enslaved people legally treated as property.

short: A dealer in clothing or small sewing goods.
note: In American usage, an outfitter selling men’s clothes and accessories; in British usage, a seller of sewing notions such as needles, thread, and buttons.

short: An excessive or salacious interest in sexual matters.
note: The quality of being prurient: an immoderate curiosity or desire, especially one directed toward sexual subjects.

short: An assistant at religious rites; also a devoted follower.
note: Originally an attendant helping the clergy during worship. The word also denotes a pupil, disciple, or close assistant to a leader.

short: Plain-woven cloth made with dyed yarn, usually cotton.
note: A fabric woven from yarn dyed before weaving, commonly associated with checks or stripes and used for clothing and household textiles.

short: An implement or apparatus for strangulation.
note: Also spelled garrote: a device used to kill by constricting the neck, including the apparatus historically employed in judicial executions.

short: Shaping stone by striking off flakes.
note: Breaking pieces from flint or another suitable stone with controlled blows to form an edge or implement.

short: Departing from accepted doctrine or conventional belief.
note: Unorthodox in opinion or practice: differing from an established teaching, religious doctrine, or accepted standard.

short: A message sent by wireless telegraphy.
note: A telegram transmitted by radio rather than along a wire.

short: A metal alloy whose chief ingredient is tin.
note: A family of tin-based alloys used for vessels and household utensils. Older pewter often contained lead; the word can also describe its dull bluish-gray color.

short: A hoofed mammal.
note: A mammal with hooves, such as a deer, horse, pig, or rhinoceros. The term groups animals by this bodily feature rather than naming a single species.

short: Rows of columns.
note: Regularly spaced columns, usually carrying the structure above them, such as a roof or entablature.

short: The ornate classical column order with leafy capitals.
note: One of the Greek architectural orders, distinguished by elaborate column capitals carved with acanthus leaves.

short: Notched like the battlements of a castle.
note: Also spelled crenellated: having a repeated pattern of raised sections and intervening gaps, as along a fortified wall.

short: A vivid red or crimson color.
note: A rich red pigment traditionally made from cochineal, and the name of the color produced by it.

short: The horizontal structural piece above a doorway or window.
note: A beam or slab spanning an opening and generally supporting the weight of the construction above it.

short: Simple beds or straw-filled mattresses.
note: In this older bedding sense, a pallet is a small or makeshift bed, especially a mattress stuffed with straw.

short: Breeding between relatively unrelated individuals.
note: Introducing comparatively unrelated hereditary stock into a breeding line, rather than breeding within a close lineage.

short: Communication and control in living and mechanical systems.
note: An interdisciplinary field comparing the regulation of systems such as brains, nervous systems, and machines, especially how information is used to control their behavior.

short: Specialists in the behavior of projectiles and firearms.
note: Experts in ballistics, including investigators who examine firearm evidence to establish how a weapon was used.

short: Of the Old Stone Age.
note: Relating to the earliest broad period of stone-tool cultures, characterized especially by chipped stone implements. The name combines Greek roots for “old” and “stone.”

short: A repeated chant or extended recital.
note: Originally a sequence of prayers alternating between a leader and a congregation; more broadly, a repetitive chant or a long enumeration.

short: An archaic word for virginity.
note: A dated term for a woman’s virginity, also historically used for the hymen. Its ending is related to “-hood,” denoting a condition or state.

short: A policy of leaving people free from interference.
note: French for “let do”: the doctrine that government should intervene minimally in economic life, or more generally an attitude of deliberate noninterference.

short: Preventive, especially against disease or infection.
note: Describing a precaution intended to avert harm before it occurs; in medical usage, a measure intended to prevent illness or its spread.

short: Confections made from nuts and sugar.
note: Sweets in which nuts are cooked with sugar; familiar forms include crisp sugared almonds and soft brown-sugar patties containing pecans.

short: Carrying a boat and its cargo over land.
note: The overland transfer of a boat or goods between waterways or around an obstruction such as a waterfall or rapids; also the path used for that transfer.

short: Roughly chipped flints once proposed as very early tools.
note: Crude chipped stones, especially flints, historically proposed as implements older than Paleolithic hand axes. Their status as human artifacts became controversial because similar shapes could be produced by natural processes.

sources.label: Muthana and Ellen: The Great Eolith Debate (2020)

short: A sailor’s shortened form of topgallant.
note: The topgallant is the mast section above the topmast. A topgallant yard is the horizontal spar carrying a square sail at that height.

short: Relating to psychiatric treatment assisted by sedative drugs.
note: Narcotherapy is a historical psychiatric technique using sedative drugs to produce a relaxed, more communicative state during treatment.

short: Rendered animal fat used in candles and soap.
note: Fat obtained chiefly from cattle or sheep and processed for uses including candle-making, soap, and lubrication.

short: Nails approximately three inches long.
note: A tenpenny nail is a nail about three inches (7.6 centimeters) long. The traditional penny designation derives from an older system of pricing nails by the hundred.

short: A wind instrument made from a row of graduated pipes.
note: An instrument formed from several short pipes of different lengths, joined with their open ends in a row so that the player can blow across them.

short: Soldiers originally equipped to throw grenades.
note: Members of infantry units originally armed with hand grenades; the designation survived in regiments after that original specialized role changed.

short: A religious ascetic or mendicant.
note: From Arabic faqīr, “poor”: a term for a Muslim religious mendicant, also used in English for Hindu ascetics or itinerant wonder-workers.

short: A thin covering; also an old term for a hairnet.
note: The word can mean a membrane enclosing part of the body. In historical dress, it also names a close-fitting cap or net used to hold the hair.

short: The tracks or other traces left by an animal.
note: Signs by which an animal can be followed, including footprints, scent, and droppings. The word comes through Afrikaans from Dutch.

short: A cart or wagon for hauling heavy goods.
note: A vehicle used to carry goods, often with a low bed and no sides. A dray horse is a horse used to draw such loads.

short: Forsaken, lonely, or desolate.
note: A literary word related to “forlorn,” used for something abandoned or left in a desolate condition.

short: Extremely light, delicate, or insubstantial.
note: Originally the fine strands or film of a spider’s web; also a very light fabric, or anything suggesting its thinness and delicacy.

short: The Roman goddess associated with marriage and childbirth.
note: The wife of Jupiter and queen of the Roman gods, especially associated with women, marriage, and childbirth.

short: Charles Darwin, the naturalist associated with natural selection.
note: Darwin’s The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex (1871) extended his evolutionary account to human origins and developed his discussion of sexual selection.

sources.label: Darwin Correspondence Project: The Descent of Man

short: Junctions through which nerve cells communicate.
note: A synapse is the junction at which a nerve impulse is conveyed from one neuron to another.

short: Relating to glands that release hormones into the bloodstream.
note: Endocrine glands secrete their products internally, rather than through ducts; their hormones help regulate bodily functions.

short: The tailbone at the lower end of the spine.
note: A small bone at the base of the spinal column, usually formed from four fused vertebrae.

short: A low protective wall along an exposed edge.
note: A wall or railing at the edge of a roof, platform, or bridge, serving as a barrier or protection.

short: Somewhat salty, as where fresh water mixes with seawater.
note: Describing water with some salt in it, commonly produced by the mixing of river water and seawater near a coast.

short: The internal organs of the body.
note: The plural of viscus, especially used collectively for organs within the trunk, such as the heart, liver, and intestines.

short: Members of the Catholic Order of Preachers.
note: The religious order founded by St. Dominic and confirmed by Pope Honorius III in 1216. Its work centers on preaching, supported by study, prayer, and communal life.

sources.label: Order of Preachers: history of the order

short: French: an Indigenous person or native inhabitant.
note: French indigène means native to a country; as a noun, a person indigenous to it. In colonial usage it distinguished the population already present from European settlers.

short: An opaque, fine-grained variety of quartz.
note: A form of quartz whose crystals are too small to distinguish with the unaided eye. Jasper occurs in several colors and is used for ornamental objects.

short: A patterned, fine-grained quartz.
note: A variety of chalcedony, or finely crystalline quartz, with contrasting colors arranged in bands, cloudy patches, or mosslike patterns.

short: A variety of chalcedony used as an ornamental stone.
note: Onyx has parallel layers of contrasting colors. The material commonly called black onyx is black chalcedony, often produced by dyeing.

sources.label: GIA: identifying black opaque gem materials

short: An aromatic herb with a licorice-like scent.
note: Anise, Pimpinella anisum, is a plant in the carrot family. Its aromatic seeds are used as a flavoring; their scent resembles licorice.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Extension: anise scent and botanical distinction

short: An aromatic spice from the seeds of a ginger-family plant.
note: The fragrant fruit and seeds of Elettaria cardamomum, an Indian plant related to ginger. Its seeds are used as a spice.

short: A Pacific region including New Guinea and nearby island groups.
note: The cultural region encompassing New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji, and New Caledonia, among other islands. Its peoples have diverse languages and cultural traditions.

short: Relating to the Greek poet Homer, his age, or his poetry.
note: An adjective connecting something with Homer, the ancient Greek poet, the period associated with him, or the world of his writings.

short: Plausible but misleading or unsound reasoning.
note: An argument that appears convincing while depending on deceptive reasoning or a concealed error.

short: An altered quotation from Euripides’ Heracles.
note: From Euripides’ Heracles, called Hercules Distracted in Michael Wodhull’s translation. Heracles tells Amphitryon that he brought Cerberus up from the underworld. Wodhull’s line has “triple-head”; David’s version substitutes “fourfold head.”

sources.label: Euripides: Hercules Distracted, translated by Michael Wodhull, p. 61
